title: Keeping pigs cool in summer
subtitle: How pigs thermoregulate and what to provide when temperatures rise.
excerpt: Pigs cannot sweat. They thermoregulate only through respiration and by seeking shade and wallowing. In temperatures above 25°C, a pig with no shade, water to wallow in, or access to damp ground is in distress. Here is how to manage pigs through UK summer heat, what signs indicate a pig is overheating, and what to do.
sourceNotes: RSPCA, pig welfare in hot weather (2023). BPEX, heat stress in outdoor pigs guidance. Moredun Research Institute, pig health and welfare.

glossaryTerms.definition: A shallow depression or container filled with water or mud that pigs lie in to cool themselves. Wallowing coats the skin in wet mud, which acts as a sunscreen and cools by evaporation. A wallow is a welfare necessity in summer, not a luxury.

content.text: Pigs are more susceptible to heat stress than most farm animals. They have a small body-surface-to-mass ratio, no functional sweat glands, and a thick layer of subcutaneous fat that insulates heat in. A pig's thermoneutral zone is 16 to 22°C for adults; above 28°C they begin to show heat stress. A
is not optional in a UK summer with warm spells.
Signs of heat stress in a pig
Rapid, open-mouthed breathing (panting): the pig is using its respiratory surface to dump heat.
Skin blotching or reddening: particularly on white-skinned breeds like Large White and Landrace.
Lying on cool ground, pressing the belly and ear-skin against it: these areas have the thinnest skin and highest blood-to-surface heat transfer.
Salivation and reluctance to eat: pigs eat less in hot weather to cut down the heat from digestion.

A wallow: a shallow rubber tub, old bath, or dug area, filled with water and topped up twice daily. Muddy water is better than clean water because the mud persists as insulation and sunscreen after the pig leaves the wallow.
Shade: a solid roof or dense tree cover. Clear polycarbonate roofing offers no shade even though it is waterproof; use dark or solid corrugated sheeting over the resting area.
Cool, fresh drinking water at all times. Pigs drink up to 15 litres per day in hot weather.
Move feed and water stations to shaded areas. Standing in direct sun to eat adds to a pig's heat load.
If a pig is actively heat-stressed

Move the pig into shade immediately. Apply cool (not ice cold) water to the head, neck, and ears. Allow the pig to stand in the wallow. If the pig is recumbent and unresponsive, call your vet. Severe heat stress can lead to organ failure rapidly in pigs.
